script.opening: (You play the son, Yusuf, 16.) "Hello, I'm ringing for my mum, she doesn't speak much English so I'll translate for you. She's got tummy pain and she's been a bit down. Just tell me what you need to know and I'll ask her. It's easier this way, we do it all the time — she's right here next to me."

facts.text: 16, in Year 11, missing a lesson to do this call. Polite, helpful, a bit impatient. You translate everything for your mum — at the bank, the school, the council.

facts.topic: What Yusuf says about the tummy pain (if asked)
facts.text: "She says it hurts here (upper tummy) for a few weeks, especially after eating. No sick, no blood." Yusuf does not know much more and guesses: "Maybe it's stress."

facts.topic: What Yusuf says about her mood
facts.text: "She's been quiet, crying sometimes. Dad says she's just homesick." Yusuf changes the subject if pushed.

facts.topic: If the doctor asks about bruising or home through Yusuf
facts.text: Yusuf hesitates, then: "She bruises easily. She's fine." Fatima, in the background, says something quickly and then goes quiet.

facts.topic: If the doctor suggests a professional interpreter
facts.text: Yusuf, a bit put out: "Honestly, I can do it, it's fine." If thanked warmly and told it is the practice's normal way of making sure his mum gets the best care, he accepts: "Okay, fair enough — when?" Fatima (via Yusuf) agrees, and if asked whether she would be happy to speak to the doctor on her own with an interpreter, says yes quietly.

facts.topic: Fatima — if a professional interpreter is used and she is alone
facts.text: Fatima, 58, speaks Arabic. Burning upper tummy pain after food for six weeks, ibuprofen most days for headaches, no weight loss, no vomiting, no black stools. Low mood for months, poor sleep, no thoughts of harming herself. If asked gently whether anyone hurts her: she cries and says her husband grabs her and pushed her against a wall last month; the bruises on her arms are from that. She is afraid for herself, not for the children. She does not want police "today" but wants to know what help exists.
Moved to the UK three years ago. No regular medicines except ibuprofen from the shop. No allergies. Does not drink or smoke.

Play Yusuf as a kind, capable teenager who is used to being the family interpreter. Do NOT let him reveal the abuse — he either does not know or will not say. Only Fatima, alone with a professional interpreter, discloses. If the doctor tries to explore abuse through Yusuf, he becomes uncomfortable and says "She's fine, honestly", and Fatima says nothing more.

ice.ideas: Yusuf: "It's probably stress or her stomach."
ice.concerns: Fatima (only when alone with a professional interpreter): fear of her husband and of what will happen if she speaks up.
ice.expectations: Yusuf: "Just tell me and I'll pass it on." Fatima wants to be able to speak freely and know what help exists.

cues: "We do it all the time — it's easier this way." — Yusuf, in the opening.
"She bruises easily." — Yusuf, if asked about bruises.
Fatima (via Yusuf) is silent and then asks him to stop translating — Yusuf says "She says it's nothing" — play this if sensitive questions are asked through him.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that using a FAMILY MEMBER — especially a CHILD — as interpreter is inappropriate/unsafe (inaccurate translation, breaches confidentiality/autonomy, inappropriate burden on the child, blocks sensitive disclosure) and declines to proceed that way, arranging a PROFESSIONAL interpreter (telephone/video service) instead
Tactfully and respectfully redirects without offending: thanks the son, explains it is practice policy / best for his mum to have a professional interpreter, and avoids implying mistrust of him

Creates a way to speak with the PATIENT DIRECTLY and confidentially — with the professional interpreter and, importantly, the opportunity to speak with her ALONE for part of the consultation — to enable free disclosure

Is alert to the SAFEGUARDING/DOMESTIC-ABUSE possibility (low mood, unexplained bruising) and recognises that getting the patient alone with a professional interpreter is essential and itself a safeguarding step — never exploring abuse through a family member
Plans the clinical assessment (abdominal pain, low mood) to happen properly via the interpreter once arranged, and has domestic-abuse/support pathways and risk assessment ready if disclosure occurs
Handles the situation with cultural sensitivity and warmth — respecting the family and the son’s good intentions while protecting the patient’s autonomy, dignity and voice
Centres the PATIENT as the person being treated, ensuring her wishes/consent (e.g. whether she is happy to be seen alone) are sought via the professional interpreter, not assumed

Safety-nets and follows up: arranges the professional-interpreter appointment and a confidential review (seeing her alone), the clinical work-up, safeguarding/domestic-abuse support if needed, and documentation — ensuring she can be heard safely

worked.txt: "Thank you so much for helping your mum — that’s really kind, and I can tell you look after her. Here’s the thing though: for medical conversations we have a rule that we use a professional, trained interpreter rather than family, even brilliant ones like you. It’s partly so nothing gets lost, and partly so your mum can speak completely freely about anything — some things people don’t like to say in front of their children. It’s nothing to do with not trusting you."

"So what I’d like to do is book a proper appointment with an interpreter on the line, and have a bit of the conversation just with your mum, so she gets the privacy any patient would. Could you let her know I’m looking forward to speaking with her properly, with the interpreter, and that she’s in good hands?"

"It’s really important to me that your mum can tell me anything that’s worrying her — about her health, her mood, her home life — in her own words and in confidence. The interpreter makes that possible. That’s the safest, kindest way to look after her."

"I know it feels easier to just do it now through you, and I don’t want to make life harder — but this genuinely matters for getting her care right, so I’m going to arrange the interpreter rather than carry on this way today. I hope that’s okay."

"I’ll get an appointment booked with the interpreter very soon for her tummy pain and how she’s been feeling. When we speak, I’ll make sure there’s time for her on her own. Is there a number where I can reach HER, or a good time?"

"If your mum’s pain gets much worse, or she’s vomiting or unwell, she should be seen urgently — you can call us or 999 and we’ll get an interpreter involved even then. Thank you again for caring for her so well. Let’s make sure she gets the chance to be heard properly."

f.learning: Using a family member — especially a CHILD — as interpreter is poor and unsafe practice: it risks inaccurate/edited translation, breaches the patient’s confidentiality and autonomy, burdens the child, and — critically — blocks disclosure of sensitive or safeguarding issues. The correct approach is a PROFESSIONAL interpreter (telephone/video service), tactfully declining family/child interpreting WITHOUT offending or implying mistrust, and creating a way to speak with the PATIENT directly and confidentially — including seeing her ALONE for part of the consultation. The examinable hidden agenda is exactly why this matters here: hints of domestic abuse/relationship distress (low mood, unexplained bruising) that the patient will not disclose through her son, whose eagerness to speak for her (well-meaning or controlling) silences her. Getting her alone with a professional interpreter is itself a safeguarding action; never explore abuse via a family member. Handle it with cultural sensitivity and warmth, centre and respect the patient’s autonomy and dignity, plan the clinical assessment via the interpreter, and have domestic-abuse/support pathways ready.

knowledge.guideline: NHS England — Guidance for commissioners: interpreting and translation services in primary care (2018) · NICE PH50 — Domestic violence and abuse (2014)
knowledge.summary: Patients with limited English should have a professional interpreter; family members, and especially children, should not interpret. Seeing her alone with a professional interpreter is also the safeguarding step that makes disclosure possible.

points.t: NHS England guidance (2018) sets out that patients should have access to professional interpreting free of charge, and that family and friends — and children in particular — should not be used to interpret except where there is no alternative in an emergency.
Family interpreting risks errors and editing, breaches confidentiality, puts a burden on the child, and blocks disclosure of sensitive issues such as abuse, mental health or sexual health.

Low mood, unexplained bruising and a relative who speaks for the patient are recognised warning signs. NICE PH50 and QS116 (2016): ask about abuse only when the person is alone and it is safe, and have referral routes ready (specialist domestic abuse services, IDVA, MARAC where risk is high).

Under the Domestic Abuse Act 2021, a child who sees, hears or experiences the effects of domestic abuse is a victim in their own right. If abuse is disclosed, consider the 16-year-old son and follow child safeguarding procedures.

A 58-year-old woman with abdominal pain needs a proper history and examination via the interpreter. If symptoms are persistent (bloating, early satiety, pelvic or abdominal pain, urinary frequency), NICE suspected-cancer guidance recommends CA125, with ultrasound if ≥31 IU/mL at age 50–59. Low mood: assess using NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025).
Brief triage for immediate danger through a family member is acceptable when no alternative exists; the full consultation should not continue that way.

dg.d: Identified who was speaking; greeted the patient directly; sought her own agreement to an interpreter.
Family dynamics, the son’s role and burden, her access to a private phone.
Face-to-face appointment for abdominal examination; considers ovarian symptom questions and CA125 if persistent.
Abdominal causes, depression, and domestic abuse as a unifying explanation.
Brief emergency triage (severe pain, vomiting, bleeding, fever) is the only use of the son.
Undiagnosed abdominal pain and low mood with safeguarding cues; needs a professional-interpreter consultation.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Professional interpreter booked; time alone built in; direct contact number; domestic abuse pathways ready (NICE PH50).
Considers the son’s welfare and child safeguarding if abuse is disclosed; flags language need on the record.
Appointment within days; red-flag symptoms named; interpreters available via 111 and 999.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Noted low mood and “bumping into things” bruising as possible abuse cues, without exploring them through the child.
Son’s idea (easier this way) and expectation (quick answers); plans to elicit the patient’s own ICE via the interpreter.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Fatima (only when alone with a professional interpreter): fear of her husband and of what will happen if she speaks up — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, it’s Dr Lee from the surgery. I’m calling for Mrs Fatima Khedira — who am I speaking to?
model.why: Identifies who is on the call before sharing anything

model.text: (Son) I’m her son. She doesn’t speak much English, so I’ll translate. She’s got tummy pain and she’s been a bit down. Just tell me what you need and I’ll ask her — we do it all the time.
Thank you — it’s kind of you to help your mum, I can tell you look after her. Before we go further, could I just say hello to her myself?
model.why: Thanks the son and centres the patient

model.text: (Mrs Khedira, quietly) Hello… doctor.
Hello, Mrs Khedira. (Slowly) I would like to get an interpreter for you. An interpreter — someone who speaks your language. Is that okay?
model.why: Seeks her own agreement in simple language

model.text: (Mrs Khedira) Yes… yes. Interpreter. Okay.

(To the son) Thank you. For medical conversations, we always use a trained interpreter rather than family — even a really good translator like you. It’s partly so nothing gets lost, and partly so your mum can talk about anything in private, the same as any other patient. It’s not about trusting you — it’s how we look after everyone.
model.why: Declines family interpreting without implying mistrust

model.text: (Son) But it’s easier this way. It’s just tummy pain.

I understand it feels easier, and I don’t want to make things harder for you. But I need to hear from your mum properly to get her care right. Can I just check one thing now so I know how quickly she needs to be seen — is the pain very severe right now, or is she being sick, bleeding, or feverish?
model.why: Brief emergency triage only, then stops using the son

model.text: (Son, after asking her) No, nothing like that. It comes and goes. She’s just been tired and sad. And she’s got some bruises — she says she keeps bumping into things.
Thank you for telling me. That’s helpful for me to know — I’ll talk it through with her when we have the interpreter.
model.why: Notes the bruising cue without exploring it through the child

model.text: Here’s what I’d like to do. I’ll book your mum an appointment with a professional interpreter, face to face here at the surgery, so I can also examine her tummy. Which language would she like the interpreter to speak?
model.why: Arranges a professional interpreter and a face-to-face assessment

model.text: (Son) Her own language — I can tell the receptionist which one.

Perfect. And I’ll make sure the appointment has time for her to talk to me on her own, with just the interpreter. We do that for everyone — it gives patients privacy. Could you let her know that’s part of it?
model.why: Plans time alone as routine practice, a safeguarding step

model.text: (Son) She won’t mind. She’s nodding.
Thank you. Is there a number where I can reach your mum directly, in case we need to change the time?
model.why: Secures a direct and confidential contact route for the patient

model.text: (Son) I’ll give the receptionist her number.
You’re clearly doing a lot to help your mum. How are you finding things yourself? You’re welcome to talk to us any time too.
model.why: Acknowledges the child’s role and offers him support

model.text: (Son) I’m okay. I just worry about her.
That’s natural. You’ve done the right thing ringing. The best help now is making sure she gets the interpreter appointment.
model.why: Validates his concern and gives him a clear role

model.text: (Son) Okay. When will it be?

I’ll ask reception to book it within the next few days, with the interpreter already arranged. Until then — if her pain becomes severe or constant, she’s being sick, has a fever, or any bleeding, call us the same day or 111, and in an emergency 999. Interpreters are available on those lines too, so she can ask for one.
model.why: Specific safety-net and access to interpreting in urgent care

model.text: (Son) Okay, I’ll tell her.
Could you tell me back what happens next, so I know I’ve been clear?
(Son) You’ll book her in with an interpreter in the next few days, face to face. If the pain gets really bad or she’s sick, we ring you or 111.
Exactly. (Slowly) Mrs Khedira — interpreter appointment soon. Thank you. Goodbye.
model.why: Closes directly with the patient, respecting her dignity

model.text: (Mrs Khedira) Thank you, doctor.

(Documentation) Record: language need and interpreter flag on the record; family interpreting declined; bruising and low mood noted for exploration alone with a professional interpreter; direct contact number obtained.
model.why: Documents the need and flags it so future bookings include an interpreter

social.t: Limited English is linked to poorer access and outcomes. Adult children often become the family’s go-between, which can hide the parent’s needs.
A 16-year-old regularly interpreting for a parent may be a young carer; the local young carers’ service can support him.

legal.t: Race (including national origin) is a protected characteristic. Services must not disadvantage patients because of language; professional interpreting supports equal access.
Defines domestic abuse and recognises children affected by it as victims in their own right.
Her information is hers. Share it with family only with her consent (GMC, Confidentiality, 2017).

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024) and GMC decision-making and consent guidance (2020) expect doctors to make arrangements so patients can understand and take part, including interpreters.
Ask about abuse only when she is alone and safe; document carefully; know the local IDVA and MARAC routes (NICE PH50).

community.t: National Domestic Abuse Helpline (Refuge) and local specialist services, many with multilingual support; young carers’ services for her son.

redFlags: Severe or constant abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding or fever — same-day assessment
Unexplained bruising with low mood — consider domestic abuse, explore alone with a professional interpreter
A relative who insists on speaking for the patient — possible control; protect time alone
psychosocial: Language barrier and reliance on her son
Possible abuse or relationship distress at home
The son’s burden as a young interpreter
ice: Son’s idea: it’s easier if he translates
Hidden concern: something at home she cannot say in front of her child
Expectation: a quick answer through the son — needed: a private consultation with a professional interpreter

playbook.diagnosis: “I can’t yet say what’s causing your mum’s pain or low mood. To find out properly, I need to talk with her in her own language and examine her.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It’s like a game of whispers — even the best translator loses a little. A trained interpreter makes sure every word from your mum reaches me, and every word from me reaches her.”

management.reflectIce: “You want to make this easy for your mum, and that’s really kind. The easiest thing for her in the long run is a proper appointment where she can talk freely.”
management.psychosocial: Protect her voice and privacy; support the son without making him responsible; flag language need so every future appointment has an interpreter.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face appointment within days with a professional interpreter; abdominal examination
Time alone with the patient as routine; ask about home safety, mood and bruising then
Domestic abuse pathways ready (NICE PH50): specialist services, IDVA, MARAC; child safeguarding if disclosed
safetyNet: Severe pain, vomiting, fever or bleeding — same-day, 111 or 999; interpreters available
Direct contact number for the patient; interpreter flag on the record

pitfalls.intro: This station is about who holds the conversation. It is failed by carrying on through the son, by exploring sensitive cues through him, or by refusing so bluntly that the family disengages.

items.fail: Taking the full history through the 16-year-old son.
items.why: Family and child interpreting breaches confidentiality and blocks disclosure; NHS England guidance expects professional interpreters.
items.fix: Brief emergency triage only, then arrange a professional interpreter.

items.fail: Asking the son about the bruises or problems at home.
items.why: If abuse is present, questioning through a family member can raise the risk to both of them.
items.fix: Note it, say you will discuss it with her, and plan time alone with the interpreter (NICE PH50).

items.fail: Implying the son is not trusted.
items.why: It offends the family and reduces the chance she attends.
items.fix: “It’s how we look after every patient — it’s nothing to do with trusting you.”

items.fail: Never speaking to the patient herself.
items.why: She is the patient. Even a simple greeting and consent in plain English respects her dignity.
items.fix: “Hello, Mrs Khedira — an interpreter, someone who speaks your language. Is that okay?”

items.fail: Ending without a date, a direct contact number, or a safety-net.
items.why: A deferred consultation without a plan is a safety risk.
items.fix: Appointment within days, her own phone number, red-flag symptoms, and interpreters available on 111/999.

items.fail: Forgetting the abdominal pain in a 58-year-old woman.
items.why: The safeguarding focus should not crowd out a clinical assessment.
items.fix: Book face to face for examination; ask about persistent bloating and satiety.

items.why: The next appointment will repeat the same problem.
items.fix: Add an interpreter flag and preferred language to the record.

avoid.dont: “Can you ask your mum where the bruises came from?”
avoid.instead: “Thank you — I’ll talk that through with her when the interpreter is with us.”
avoid.why: Exploring possible abuse through a child can put both at risk and silences her.

avoid.dont: “I can’t speak to you, I need an interpreter. Goodbye.”
avoid.instead: “Thank you for helping. For medical conversations we always use a trained interpreter — here’s what happens next.”
avoid.why: A blunt refusal alienates the family and leaves no plan or safety-net.

avoid.instead: “Which language would she like the interpreter to speak?”
avoid.why: Judgement about language damages trust and cuts against equal access (Equality Act 2010).

Low mood, unexplained bruising and a relative who speaks for the patient are recognised warning signs. NICE PH50 and QS116 (2016): ask about abuse only when the person is alone and it is safe, and have referral routes ready (specialist domestic abuse services, IDVA, MARAC where risk is high).

A 58-year-old woman with abdominal pain needs a proper history and examination via the interpreter. If symptoms are persistent (bloating, early satiety, pelvic or abdominal pain, urinary frequency), NICE suspected-cancer guidance recommends CA125, with ultrasound if ≥31 IU/mL at age 50–59. Low mood: assess using NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025).
Brief triage for immediate danger through a family member is acceptable when no alternative exists; the full consultation should not continue that way.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Identified who was speaking; greeted the patient directly; sought her own agreement to an interpreter.
Family dynamics, the son’s role and burden, her access to a private phone.
Noted low mood and “bumping into things” bruising as possible abuse cues, without exploring them through the child.
Son’s idea (easier this way) and expectation (quick answers); plans to elicit the patient’s own ICE via the interpreter.
Face-to-face appointment for abdominal examination; considers ovarian symptom questions and CA125 if persistent.
Abdominal causes, depression, and domestic abuse as a unifying explanation.
Brief emergency triage (severe pain, vomiting, bleeding, fever) is the only use of the son.
Undiagnosed abdominal pain and low mood with safeguarding cues; needs a professional-interpreter consultation.
Professional interpreter booked; time alone built in; direct contact number; domestic abuse pathways ready (NICE PH50).
Considers the son’s welfare and child safeguarding if abuse is disclosed; flags language need on the record.
Appointment within days; red-flag symptoms named; interpreters available via 111 and 999.

social.t: Limited English is linked to poorer access and outcomes. Adult children often become the family’s go-between, which can hide the parent’s needs.
A 16-year-old regularly interpreting for a parent may be a young carer; the local young carers’ service can support him.

legal.t: Race (including national origin) is a protected characteristic. Services must not disadvantage patients because of language; professional interpreting supports equal access.
Defines domestic abuse and recognises children affected by it as victims in their own right.
Her information is hers. Share it with family only with her consent (GMC, Confidentiality, 2017).

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024) and GMC decision-making and consent guidance (2020) expect doctors to make arrangements so patients can understand and take part, including interpreters.
Ask about abuse only when she is alone and safe; document carefully; know the local IDVA and MARAC routes (NICE PH50).

community.t: National Domestic Abuse Helpline (Refuge) and local specialist services, many with multilingual support; young carers’ services for her son.

redFlags: Severe or constant abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding or fever — same-day assessment
Unexplained bruising with low mood — consider domestic abuse, explore alone with a professional interpreter
A relative who insists on speaking for the patient — possible control; protect time alone
psychosocial: Language barrier and reliance on her son
Possible abuse or relationship distress at home
The son’s burden as a young interpreter
ice: Son’s idea: it’s easier if he translates
Hidden concern: something at home she cannot say in front of her child
Expectation: a quick answer through the son — needed: a private consultation with a professional interpreter

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “I can’t yet say what’s causing your mum’s pain or low mood. To find out properly, I need to talk with her in her own language and examine her.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “It’s like a game of whispers — even the best translator loses a little. A trained interpreter makes sure every word from your mum reaches me, and every word from me reaches her.”

management.reflectIce: “You want to make this easy for your mum, and that’s really kind. The easiest thing for her in the long run is a proper appointment where she can talk freely.”
management.psychosocial: Protect her voice and privacy; support the son without making him responsible; flag language need so every future appointment has an interpreter.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face appointment within days with a professional interpreter; abdominal examination
Time alone with the patient as routine; ask about home safety, mood and bruising then
Domestic abuse pathways ready (NICE PH50): specialist services, IDVA, MARAC; child safeguarding if disclosed
safetyNet: Severe pain, vomiting, fever or bleeding — same-day, 111 or 999; interpreters available
Direct contact number for the patient; interpreter flag on the record

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is about who holds the conversation. It is failed by carrying on through the son, by exploring sensitive cues through him, or by refusing so bluntly that the family disengages.

items.fail: Taking the full history through the 16-year-old son.
items.why: Family and child interpreting breaches confidentiality and blocks disclosure; NHS England guidance expects professional interpreters.
items.fix: Brief emergency triage only, then arrange a professional interpreter.

items.fail: Asking the son about the bruises or problems at home.
items.why: If abuse is present, questioning through a family member can raise the risk to both of them.
items.fix: Note it, say you will discuss it with her, and plan time alone with the interpreter (NICE PH50).

items.fail: Implying the son is not trusted.
items.why: It offends the family and reduces the chance she attends.
items.fix: “It’s how we look after every patient — it’s nothing to do with trusting you.”

items.fail: Never speaking to the patient herself.
items.why: She is the patient. Even a simple greeting and consent in plain English respects her dignity.
items.fix: “Hello, Mrs Khedira — an interpreter, someone who speaks your language. Is that okay?”

items.fail: Ending without a date, a direct contact number, or a safety-net.
items.why: A deferred consultation without a plan is a safety risk.
items.fix: Appointment within days, her own phone number, red-flag symptoms, and interpreters available on 111/999.

items.fail: Forgetting the abdominal pain in a 58-year-old woman.
items.why: The safeguarding focus should not crowd out a clinical assessment.
items.fix: Book face to face for examination; ask about persistent bloating and satiety.

items.why: The next appointment will repeat the same problem.
items.fix: Add an interpreter flag and preferred language to the record.
